common_name: Summer Jewel Lavender Salvia (Compact Early-Blooming Hummingbird Sage)

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 sow March-May or September for a fall planting. Summer Jewel Lavender blooms several weeks earlier from seed than standard-sized Salvia coccinea and stays compact at 18-24 inches.

directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil; Summer Jewel Lavender is drought-tolerant once established and blooms most freely in full sun but performs well in partial shade in zone 9. It rounds out the All-America Selections-winning Summer Jewel series alongside Red and Pink, offering the same compact, early-blooming, heat-tolerant habit of tropical sage in a soft, cool lavender-blue that reads differently in the border than its warm-toned siblings, borne on whorled spikes atop upright, well-branched plants from late spring to frost. Like the rest of the series it is bred from a Gulf Coast and Caribbean native wildflower that normally reaches 3-4 feet, condensed here into a garden-scaled size that still draws hummingbirds and butterflies reliably. It self-seeds readily in zone 9, and established plants need little beyond an occasional deep watering during extended dry spells.
sources: All-America Selections — Salvia Summer Jewel series

common_name: Cora Cascade Vinca (Trailing Disease-Resistant Annual Vinca)

planting.note: Transplant out after soil has warmed and all frost danger has passed, ideally two to three weeks after the last frost; Cora Cascade is a trailing habit selection bred for the same aerial and soil-borne disease resistance as the upright Cora series.

directions: Transplant into well-drained soil or containers in full sun after the soil has warmed, since cool, wet conditions invite the root and stem rot that vinca is otherwise notably prone to. Cora Cascade brings the upright Cora series' breakthrough resistance to Phytophthora aerial blight and root rot to a low, trailing habit suited to hanging baskets, window boxes, and groundcover use, spilling over container edges in a dense mound of glossy foliage covered in flat, five-petaled blooms from late spring through the first frost. It shrugs off heat, humidity, and drought once established, needing far less water than the disease-prone open-pollinated vincas of decades past, and rarely requires deadheading since spent flowers are self-cleaning. Avoid overhead watering and overly rich, waterlogged soil, both of which undercut its main advantage over older vinca types.

common_name: Supertunia Mini Vista Indigo (Compact Small-Flowered Spreading Petunia)

planting.note: Transplant out after the danger of frost has passed; Mini Vista is a compact, small-flowered, self-cleaning spreading petunia that fills containers and beds without the sprawling reach of standard Supertunias.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil or containers in full sun; regular deadheading is not needed since flowers are self-cleaning, though a light trim mid-season refreshes tired growth. Mini Vista Indigo is a compact member of the Supertunia line bred for smaller flowers and a tighter mound than standard-sized Supertunias, making it well suited to smaller containers, hanging baskets, and mixed combination plantings where a large-flowered, fast-spreading petunia would overwhelm its neighbors. It covers itself in small, rich indigo-purple blooms from spring through frost and holds up well to heat and summer rain without the flower rot that troubles older, large-flowered grandiflora petunias. Feed regularly through the season, since container plantings deplete nutrients quickly, and water whenever the top inch of soil dries out.
sources: Proven Winners — Supertunia Mini Vista series

planting.note: Transplant out after the danger of frost has passed; Surefire Rose tolerates both full sun and considerable shade without the leggy stretching common in older fibrous begonias grown outside their preferred light range.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil or containers in a site ranging from full sun to fairly deep shade; Surefire Rose is bred for that unusual light-range flexibility, holding a tidy, mounded, self-branching habit and steady bloom whether it lands in a sun-baked bed or a shaded porch pot. It bears rounded clusters of bright rose-pink flowers continuously from spring through frost above glossy, bronze-green foliage, needing no deadheading since spent blooms drop cleanly on their own. It is markedly more heat- and rain-tolerant than older wax begonias, resisting the flower and foliage melt that summer downpours cause in less vigorous types, and it stands up to Gulf Coast summer humidity without special care beyond regular watering and an occasional balanced feeding.
